name: Krzysztof Kieślowski
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: by age 26 (1967) Kieślowski was still a student at the Łódź Film School (attended 1964–1968); his first significant documentary (Murarz) came in 1973 and first feature (The Scar) in 1976.
early_history_summary: Kieślowski grew up in small Polish towns, attending a firefighters' school briefly before enrolling in the College for Theatre Technicians in Warsaw. He was rejected twice from the Łódź Film School before being accepted on his third attempt in 1964, graduating in 1968.
family_context_summary: Son of Barbara and Roman Kieślowski, an engineer and tuberculosis patient; the family moved frequently for the father's treatment.
evidence_summary: Kieślowski's early career was spent in training at the Łódź Film School, one of Europe's premier film institutions, but he produced no material milestone before age 26. His student films (Tramwaj, 1966; Koncert życzeń, 1967) were school exercises, and his breakthrough documentaries and features came in his 30s.

name: Robin Li
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: by age 26 (Nov 1994) Li had just completed his MS in computer science at the University at Buffalo; his RankDex search algorithm was created in 1996 (age 28) and Baidu was founded in 2000 (age 32).
early_history_summary: Born to factory-worker parents in Yangquan, Shanxi Province, Li earned a bachelor's in information management from Peking University in 1991, then pursued graduate studies in computer science at the University at Buffalo, completing his MS in 1994. He subsequently worked at Dow Jones and Infoseek before founding Baidu.
family_context_summary: Born to factory-worker parents in Yangquan, Shanxi; the fourth of five children and the only son. Grew up during the Cultural Revolution in an impoverished city.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Parents were factory workers with no apparent tech background.
evidence_summary: Li's path to success was gradual: Peking University undergraduate, Buffalo MS, then industry experience at Dow Jones and Infoseek before his 1996 RankDex breakthrough and 2000 Baidu founding. No material milestone occurred by age 26; his major achievements came in his late 20s and 30s.

name: Martin Karplus
milestone_by_age_26: Received PhD in chemistry from Caltech under two-time Nobel laureate Linus Pauling in 1953 at age 23; Pauling called him 'my most brilliant student.'
early_history_summary: Born in Vienna to a family of distinguished doctors and medical researchers, Karplus fled with his family to the U.S. in 1938 after the Anschluss. He published his first academic paper at age 17 and entered Harvard College on a Westinghouse scholarship. After graduating from Harvard he moved to Caltech for his doctoral work under Linus Pauling, completing his PhD by age 23.
family_context_summary: Born into an accomplished Jewish family in Vienna; both grandparents had scientific achievements. His family fled Nazi-occupied Austria in 1938 and settled in the Boston area, where his parents prioritized education and moved to Newton for better schools.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family of distinguished doctors and medical researchers; his grandfather studied at the University of Vienna and his grandmother studied economics. The family assumed Karplus would follow the medical profession.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Harvard undergraduate, Caltech PhD under Pauling, refugee from Nazis, scientific family, early publication
evidence_summary: Karplus benefited from an elite educational pipeline: Harvard College on scholarship, then Caltech for his PhD under Linus Pauling, who called him 'my most brilliant student.' He published his first academic paper at 17 and conducted ornithological field research in Alaska as a high school student. His family's scientific background and refugee experience shaped his early scientific trajectory. By age 23 he had a Caltech doctorate, and by 26 he was a postdoctoral fellow at Oxford.
starting_point: Born in Vienna in 1930 to an accomplished Jewish family of doctors and medical researchers; fled Nazi-occupied Austria in 1938 and settled in suburban Boston, where parents prioritized education.
current_position: Died December 28, 2024 at age 94 in Cambridge, Massachusetts; was the Theodore William Richards Professor of Chemistry, Emeritus, at Harvard University and Nobel Laureate in Chemistry (2013).

trajectory.event: Entered Harvard College on Westinghouse and Harvard National scholarships and published his first academic paper.
Received PhD in chemistry from Caltech under Linus Pauling, who called him 'my most brilliant student.'
Conducted postdoctoral research at Oxford University before returning to the U.S.
Joined the faculty at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.
Became Professor of Chemistry at Harvard University.
Awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for development of multiscale models for complex chemical systems.
Died on December 28 at his home in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

name: Richard Dawkins
milestone_by_age_26: Completed DPhil at Oxford University under Nobel laureate Niko Tinbergen in 1966 at age 25, then appointed assistant professor of zoology at UC Berkeley in 1967.
early_history_summary: Born in Nairobi, Kenya to a British colonial agricultural civil servant from a landed gentry family in Oxfordshire, Dawkins returned to England at age 8. He attended Oundle School, where an inspirational biology teacher sparked his interest, then went up to Oxford in 1959. He studied under Niko Tinbergen, completing his DPhil in 1966 at age 25.
family_context_summary: Son of Clinton John Dawkins, an agricultural civil servant in the British Colonial Service, and Jean Mary Vyvyan (née Ladner). The Dawkins family were landed gentry from Oxfordshire, owning a farm since 1726. His father read Botany at Oxford.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a biologist who read Botany at Oxford before joining the Colonial Service; Dawkins followed a similar scientific path, partly influenced by his father's background.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Oxford education, Tinbergen mentorship, landed gentry family, father a biologist, Oundle School
evidence_summary: Dawkins's early trajectory was shaped by Oxford's elite academic ecosystem: he entered Balliol College in 1959, came under the influence of Nobel laureate Niko Tinbergen, and completed his DPhil by age 25. His father's botanical training at Oxford and the family's landed gentry status provided domain proximity and financial security. An inspirational biology teacher at Oundle School also played a role. By 26 he was an assistant professor at Berkeley.
starting_point: Born in Nairobi, Kenya in 1941 to a British colonial agricultural civil servant from an Oxfordshire landed gentry family that had owned a farm since 1726; returned to England at age 8.
current_position: Emeritus fellow of New College, Oxford; was the first Simonyi Professor for the Public Understanding of Science (1995–2008); remains active as a public intellectual and author at age 84.

trajectory.event: Began undergraduate studies at Balliol College, Oxford University.
Graduated from Oxford and began graduate research under Niko Tinbergen.
Completed DPhil at Oxford under Nobel laureate Niko Tinbergen, studying animal behavior and ethology.
Appointed assistant professor of zoology at the University of California, Berkeley.
Published The Selfish Gene, introducing the gene-centered view of evolution and the concept of the meme.
Named the first Simonyi Professor for the Public Understanding of Science at Oxford University.
Published The God Delusion, becoming a leading figure of the New Atheism movement.

name: Sting
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: by age 26 (Oct 1977) Sting had just formed The Police in January 1977 but had no chart success; the band's first UK chart-topping album came in 1978–1979. Before that he was a schoolteacher and local musician in Newcastle.
early_history_summary: Born Gordon Sumner in Wallsend, Northumberland to a milkman and a hairdresser, Sting worked odd jobs before qualifying as a teacher at Northern Counties College of Education (1971–1974). He taught at St Paul's First School for two years while playing in local jazz and rock bands including the Phoenix Jazzmen and Last Exit. He joined The Police in January 1977 at age 25.
family_context_summary: Eldest of four children of Ernest Matthew Sumner, a milkman and former fitter at an engineering works, and Audrey (née Cowell), a hairdresser. Grew up near Wallsend's shipyards in a working-class environment.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Parents had no music industry background.
evidence_summary: Sting's path to fame was gradual: he trained as a teacher, taught for two years, and played in local Newcastle bands before forming The Police at 25. The band's commercial breakthrough came in 1978–1979, when Sting was 27–28. No material milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Yang Hak-seon
milestone_by_age_26: Won gold in vault at the 2011 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Tokyo at age 19, becoming the first South Korean world champion in gymnastics; followed by Olympic gold in vault at the 2012 London Games.
early_history_summary: Born in Gwangju, South Korea to a poor family, Yang started gymnastics at age 9 at Gwangcheon Elementary School, where older teammates looked after him while his parents worked. He progressed through Gwangju Physical Education Middle and High School, specializing in vault. His coach Oh Sang-jin guided him through adolescence, including bringing him back when he ran away from training due to family hardship. By his mid-teens he was already practicing senior-level vault technique.
family_context_summary: Born into severe poverty in Gwangju; both parents were injured and the family lived in a makeshift greenhouse in a rural area. Yang sent his modest training stipend home to support his family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No family background in gymnastics or sports.
primary_early_advantage_tags: poverty, early gymnastics training, specialized sports schools, coach mentorship, natural vaulting talent
evidence_summary: Yang's trajectory from poverty to Olympic gold was driven by early specialization in gymnastics from age 9, sustained coaching by Oh Sang-jin, and a natural aptitude for vaulting that led to a skill named after him by the FIG. He trained through Gwangju Physical Education Middle and High School and the Korean national training system. His family's extreme poverty and his parents' injuries created both urgency and hardship, but the Korean sports pipeline provided the institutional structure for his talent to develop. By 19 he was world champion and Olympic gold medalist.
starting_point: Born in 1992 in Gwangju, South Korea to a poor family; both parents were injured and the family lived in a makeshift greenhouse in a rural area, relying on Yang's modest training stipend.
current_position: Retired from competitive gymnastics in September 2025; Olympic gold medalist (2012) and two-time World champion in vault, with a vault technique named after him by the FIG.

trajectory.event: Began gymnastics training at Gwangcheon Elementary School in Gwangju.
Won gold in vault at the World Artistic Gymnastics Championship in Tokyo, becoming South Korea's first world champion in gymnastics.
Won Olympic gold in vault at the London Games, the first Olympic gymnastics gold for South Korea.
Won gold in vault at the Asian Games in Incheon.
Competed at the Tokyo Olympic Games.
Retired from competitive gymnastics in September 2025.

name: Andre Geim
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: by age 26 (Oct 1984) Geim was a PhD student at the Institute of Solid State Physics in Chernogolovka; his PhD was completed in 1987 (age 29) and the graphene discovery came in 2004 (age 46).
early_history_summary: Born in Sochi, Russia to German-origin parents who were both engineers, Geim graduated from school with a gold medal and studied at the Moscow Engineering and Physics Institute (MIFI). He began his PhD at the Institute of Solid State Physics after graduating, working on helicon resonance in metals. His PhD thesis was completed in 1987.
family_context_summary: Born to Konstantin Alekseyevich Geim and Nina Nikolayevna Bayer in Sochi, Russia; both parents were engineers of German descent.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were engineers, providing a technical household environment, though no specific domain transfer is documented.
evidence_summary: Geim's path to the Nobel Prize was long and indirect: he studied at MIFI, completed a PhD in 1987 on a topic he described as scientifically dead, then did postdocs in the West before securing a position in the Netherlands and eventually Manchester. The graphene discovery came in 2004 when he was 46. No material milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Boris Gelfand
milestone_by_age_26: Won the USSR Junior Chess Championship in 1985 at age 17 with 9/11, after already winning the Sokolsky Memorial (1983, age 15) and consecutive Belarusian Chess Championships (1984, 1985); became a grandmaster at 21 in 1989.
early_history_summary: Born in Minsk, Byelorussian SSR to engineer parents, Gelfand received a chess book from his father at age 5 and showed immediate talent. He was coached by Eduard Zelkind (1974–1979), Tamara Golovey, and then IM Albert Kapengut for twelve years. He attended the Tigran Petrosian School from 1980 to 1983. By his mid-teens he was winning major tournaments, including the Sokolsky Memorial at 15 and the USSR Junior Championship at 17.
family_context_summary: Born to Belarusian Jewish parents Abram and Nella Gelfand, both engineers, in Minsk. Described as a 'typical intelligent family' that prioritized education and development.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Abram was an engineer who frequently traveled on business and bought Boris a chess book (Journey to the Chess Kingdom) at age 5, igniting his interest. No family chess background is documented, but the family supported his chess education.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet chess pipeline, Tigran Petrosian School, Kapengut coaching, early start at 5, USSR Junior champion
evidence_summary: Gelfand's early chess dominance was built on the Soviet chess pipeline: he started at 5, received sustained coaching from IM Albert Kapengut for 12 years, and attended the Tigran Petrosian School. His parents, both engineers, supported his development in a culture that valued chess mastery. By 15 he won the Sokolsky Memorial, by 17 the USSR Junior Championship, and by 21 he was a grandmaster ranked in the world's top 40. The depth of Soviet chess training infrastructure was a decisive early advantage.
starting_point: Born in 1968 in Minsk, Byelorussian SSR to Belarusian Jewish parents who were both engineers; described as a 'typical intelligent family' that prioritized education and development.
current_position: Active as Israel's top-rated classical chess player (rated ~2641 as of 2025); challenged Viswanathan Anand for the World Chess Championship in 2012; has spent most of his life ranked among the world's top-20 players.

trajectory.event: Won the Sokolsky Memorial chess tournament with 11.5/16 points, undefeated.
Won the USSR Junior Chess Championship with 9/11, establishing himself as a top junior player.
Became European Junior Champion and entered the FIDE world top-100 rating list.
Awarded the chess grandmaster title and placed joint second in the 56th Soviet Chess Championship.
Reached world No. 3 ranking, finishing second to Kasparov at Linares and Dortmund, and sharing first at the Manila Interzonal.
Challenged Viswanathan Anand for the World Chess Championship, losing narrowly in the final game.

name: Albert Speer
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: by age 26 (July 1960) Speer was still studying architecture at the Technical University of Munich; he won his first international prize in 1964 (age 30) and founded his own firm the same year.
early_history_summary: Born in Berlin in 1934 as the eldest son of Hitler's chief architect Albert Speer Sr., Speer Jr. took a carpentry apprenticeship, completed night-school high school, and studied architecture at TU Munich. He worked at firms in Germany, Sweden, and Turkey before founding his own practice in Frankfurt in 1964.
family_context_summary: Eldest of six children of Albert Speer, Hitler's chief architect and later Minister of Armaments. The family lived near Hitler's Bavarian mountain retreat in housing for the Nazi elite during his childhood. His father was imprisoned at Nuremberg when Speer Jr. was young.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father and grandfather were both architects; Speer Jr. followed in the family tradition, though he claimed his decision was unrelated to his father's legacy.
evidence_summary: Speer Jr.'s career developed slowly: carpentry apprenticeship, night-school diploma, then architecture studies at TU Munich. His first international prize and own firm both came in 1964 when he was 30. The burden of his father's Nazi legacy may have shaped his career path, but no material milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Ludovico Scarfiotti
milestone_by_age_26: Won the first of three consecutive Italian Hillclimb championships in 1957 at age 23–24, after winning his class in the 1956 Mille Miglia; later won the 24 Hours of Le Mans (1963) and the Italian Grand Prix (1966) with Ferrari.
early_history_summary: Born in Turin into a wealthy industrial family with deep ties to Fiat—his grandfather was co-founder and first president of Fiat, and his father Luigi was a racing driver who finished third in the 1932 Mille Miglia. Scarfiotti was associated with cars from his youth and began racing in 1953 at age 20, driving a Fiat 1100 to class victory in the 1956 Mille Miglia before dominating Italian hillclimbing from 1957 to 1959.
family_context_summary: Born into a wealthy industrial family in Turin; grandson of Lodovico Scarfiotti, co-founder and first president of Fiat, and nephew of Giovanni Agnelli. His father Luigi Scarfiotti was a racing driver and member of the Italian Parliament who made a fortune as a cement manufacturer.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Luigi Scarfiotti was an amateur racing driver who competed with Scuderia Ferrari in the 1930s, finishing third in the 1932 Mille Miglia. Grandfather co-founded Fiat. The family's deep automotive and industrial connections provided direct domain immersion from birth.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Fiat heir, racing driver father, Turin motorsport hub, Ferrari connection, wealthy industrial family
evidence_summary: Scarfiotti's racing career was built on extraordinary inherited advantages: his grandfather co-founded Fiat, his father was a racing driver, and his uncle was Fiat's president. He grew up around cars in Turin, Italy's motorsport capital, and had direct access to Ferrari through family connections. He began racing in 1953, won his class in the Mille Miglia by 1956, and dominated Italian hillclimbing from 1957–1959. His family's wealth and industrial connections were directly catalytic to his early racing career.
starting_point: Born in 1933 in Turin, Italy into a wealthy industrial family; grandson of Fiat co-founder Lodovico Scarfiotti, son of racing driver Luigi Scarfiotti, and nephew of Fiat president Giovanni Agnelli.
current_position: Died June 8, 1968 at age 34 in Berchtesgaden, West Germany, from injuries sustained while hillclimbing in a Porsche 910; final role: Ferrari and Cooper Formula One driver, European Hillclimb champion.

trajectory.event: Began competitive racing, initially driving family Fiat and OSCA cars in Italian events.
Won his class in the Mille Miglia driving a Fiat 1100.
Won the first of three consecutive Italian Hillclimb championships (1957–1959).
Signed with Ferrari as a sportscar driver, finishing fourth at the Targa Florio.
Won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with Lorenzo Bandini and the 12 Hours of Sebring with John Surtees, both driving for Ferrari.
Won the Italian Grand Prix at Monza with Ferrari, his sole Formula One victory.
Died on June 8 from injuries sustained in a hillclimb accident in a Porsche 910 near Berchtesgaden.

name: Timothy Laurence
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: by age 26 (March 1981) Laurence was a lieutenant in the Royal Navy with no independently notable milestone; his first significant recognition (mentioned in dispatches) came in 1982 at age 27, and his first ship command in 1982–1983.
early_history_summary: Born in South London to a Royal Navy commander, Laurence was educated at The New Beacon Preparatory School and Sevenoaks School before receiving a Naval Scholarship to study geography at University College, Durham. He was commissioned into the Royal Navy as a midshipman in 1973 at age 17 and promoted to sub-lieutenant, then lieutenant by 1977.
family_context_summary: Younger son of Commander Guy Stewart Laurence RN (1896–1982), a Royal Navy officer who later became a sales executive, and Barbara Alison Laurence (née Symons). The family descends patrilineally from Zaccaria Levy, an 18th-century Jewish merchant from Venice.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a Royal Navy commander, providing direct military domain exposure and likely influencing Laurence's naval career path.
evidence_summary: Laurence's naval career followed a conventional officer path: naval scholarship to Durham, commissioned at 17, gradual promotions. His first notable recognition (mentioned in dispatches for anti-IRA patrols) came at 27, and his first command at 27–28. He is primarily known for his marriage to Princess Anne and his later role as equerry to Queen Elizabeth II, neither of which occurred by age 26.

name: Türkan Saylan
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: by age 26 (Dec 1961) Saylan was still a medical student at Istanbul University Faculty of Medicine; she graduated in 1963 at age 28 and began her dermatology residency afterward. Her leprosy work started in 1976.
early_history_summary: Born in Istanbul in 1935 as the eldest child of Fasih Galip, one of Turkey's first building contractors, and Swiss-born Lili Mina Raiman (who converted to Islam and took the name Leyla). She attended Kandilli Girls' High School before entering Istanbul University Faculty of Medicine, graduating in 1963 at age 28. She completed her dermatology residency at SSK Nişantaşı Hospital (1963–1965).
family_context_summary: Born to Fasih Galip Saylan, one of Turkey's first building contractors in the republican era, and Swiss-born Lili Mina Raiman (who converted from Christianity and took the name Leyla). The family lived in Kandilli, Istanbul, in a house with a garden; five siblings had a comfortable childhood.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No family medical background is mentioned, though the family was prosperous.
evidence_summary: Saylan's medical career began late by the age-26 standard: she graduated from Istanbul Medical School in 1963 at age 28, completed her dermatology residency by 1965, and became a chief assistant at Istanbul Faculty of Medicine in 1968. Her famous leprosy work and social activism began in 1976 when she was 41. No material milestone occurred by age 26.
